{{Short description|None}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=July 2023}}
The [[governor of Louisiana]] is the [[head of government]]  of the [[U.S. state]] of [[Louisiana]]. The [[Governor (United States)|governor]] is the head of the [[Executive (government)|executive branch]] of [[Louisiana|Louisiana's state government]] and is charged with enforcing state laws.
[[Republican Party of Louisiana|Republican]] [[Jeff Landry]] has served as the current governor since January 8, 2024.

==List of governors==

===Territory of Orleans===
{{For|the period before purchase|List of colonial governors of Louisiana}}
[[Louisiana (New France)|Louisiana]] was [[Louisiana Purchase|purchased]] by the United States from France in 1803.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Van Zandt |first=Franklin K. |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_skxAAAAAIAAJ/page/n32 |title=Boundaries of the United States and the Several States: With Miscellaneous Geographic Information Concerning Areas, Altitudes, and Geographic Centers |publisher=[[United States Government Publishing Office]] |year=1976 |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=23–26 |oclc=69426475}}</ref> On October 1, 1804, [[Territory of Orleans|Orleans Territory]] was organized from the southern part of the Purchase, with the remainder being made the [[District of Louisiana]] and placed under the jurisdiction of [[Indiana Territory]].<ref>{{usstat|2|283}}</ref> The District of Louisiana would later become [[Louisiana Territory]], but after Orleans Territory became the state of Louisiana, Louisiana Territory was renamed [[Missouri Territory]].<ref>{{usstat|2|743}}</ref>

and was reconfirmed by the Senate on December 23, 1805;<ref>{{cite book |title=Senate Executive Journal, 9th Cong., 1st sess. |author=United States Senate |page=10 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044106526916&seq=14 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> November 14, 1808;<ref>{{cite book |title=Senate Executive Journal, 10th Cong., 2nd sess. |author=United States Senate |page=84 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044106526916&seq=88 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> and November 26, 1811.<ref>{{cite book |title=Senate Executive Journal, 12th Cong., 1st sess. |author=United States Senate |page=192 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044106526916&seq=194 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref>}}<br />–<br />July 30, 1812<br>{{small|(3146 days; ===State of Louisiana===
[[Louisiana]] was [[List of U.S. states by date of admission to the Union|admitted to the Union]] on April 30, 1812.<ref>{{usstat|2|701}}</ref> It seceded from the [[Union (American Civil War)|Union]] on January 26, 1861,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Secession Ordinances of 13 Confederate States |url=http://www.digitalhistory.uh.edu/disp_textbook.cfm?smtID=3&psid=3953 |url-status=live |year=2018 |last1=Mintz |first1=S. |last2=McNeil |first2=S. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905091739/http://www.digitalhistory.uh.edu/disp_textbook.cfm?smtID=3&psid=3953 |archive-date=September 5, 2015 |access-date=October 1, 2026 |website=Digital History}}</ref> and was a founding member of the [[Confederate States of America]] on February 8, 1861.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=dul1.ark:/13960/t2t44fh2r&seq=23 |page=1 |title=The Statutes at Large of the Provisional Government of the Confederate States of America |editor-last=Matthews |editor-first=James M. |year=1864 |location=Richmond, Virginia |publisher=R.M. Smith |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> However, since substantial parts of the state remained in Union hands throughout the war, there were two lines of governors elected. Following the end of the [[American Civil War]], Louisiana during [[Reconstruction era|Reconstruction]] was part of the [[Fifth Military District]], which exerted some control over governor appointments and elections.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bradley |first=Mark L. |url=https://history.army.mil/html/books/075/75-18/cmhPub_75-18.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150911212248/http://www.history.army.mil/html/books/075/75-18/cmhPub_75-18.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 11, 2015 |title=The Army and Reconstruction, 1865-1877 |publisher=[[United States Army Center of Military History]] |year=2015 |page=31 |access-date=June 20, 2019}}</ref> Louisiana was readmitted to the Union on July 9, 1868.<ref>Act authorizing readmission on ratification of 14th amendment: {{usstat|15|73}}. Proclamation of Louisiana's ratification: {{usstat|15|704}}.</ref>

The 1812 [[Constitution of Louisiana|constitution]] established the office of governor, to serve for four years{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1384|loc=1812 art. III, § 2}} starting from the fourth Monday after the election.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1385|loc=1812 art. III, § 5}} In 1845, the start date was moved to the fourth Monday of the January after the election;{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1397|loc=1845 title III, art. 40}} in 1864, it was moved to the second Monday of the January after the election;{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1436|loc=1864 title IV, art. 45}} in 1879 it was moved to the first Monday after the [[Louisiana State Legislature|General Assembly]] announced the election result;{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1481|loc=1879 art. 61}} and the 1974 Constitution changed the date, effective in 1980, to the second Monday of the March following the election.{{sfn|Kallenbach|1977|p=217}} This was amended in 1987, to become effective in 1992, to the second Monday of January.{{sfn|La. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/la/constitution/section-id-69152 art. IV, § 3]}} Governors were not allowed to succeed themselves{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1384|loc=1812 art. III, § 3}} until 1864, when the constitution held no term limits. The restriction on governors succeeding themselves was reintroduced in 1868,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1456|loc=1868 title III, art. 50}} removed in 1870,<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 14, 1870 |title=none |page=4 |newspaper=New Orleans Republican |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-orleans-republican-repeal-of-article/137021269/ |quote=The abrogation of this article renders the Governor of the State eligible for a re-election. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231218182630/https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-orleans-republican-repeal-of-article/137021269/ |archive-date=December 18, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> and again added in 1898.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1533|loc=1898 art. 63}} An amendment to the constitution passed in 1966 allowed governors to succeed themselves once before requiring a gap before they can be elected again.{{sfn|La. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/la/constitution/section-id-69152 art. IV, § 3]}} Five governors have served nonconsecutive terms. [[André B. Roman]], [[Francis T. Nicholls]], and [[Jimmie Davis]] each served two non-consecutive terms, while [[Earl Long]] and [[Edwin Edwards]] both served in three distinct stints.

In the event of a vacancy, the President of the Senate originally acted as governor.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1385|loc=1812 art. III, § 17}} The 1845 constitution created the office of [[Lieutenant Governor of Louisiana|lieutenant governor]], to be elected at the same time and manner as the governor{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1397|loc=1845 title III, art. 38}} and who would act as governor in the event of a vacancy.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1398|loc=1845 title III, art. 43}} The 1913 constitution established that the lieutenant governor would become governor in case of a vacancy.<ref name="const1913">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924030492148/page/n17 |page=14 |title=Constitution of Louisiana, 1913 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> The governor and the lieutenant governor are not officially elected on the same [[ticket (election)|ticket]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sentell |first=Will |date=May 8, 2019 |title=House Says No to Governor, Lieutenant Governor Running on Same Ticket |language=en |website=[[The Advocate (Louisiana)|The Advocate]] |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/house-says-no-to-governor-lieutenant-governor-running-on-same-ticket/article_23ede272-71d8-11e9-941d-97c0cfc7e867.html |access-date=October 27, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230927155527/https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/house-says-no-to-governor-lieutenant-governor-running-on-same-ticket/article_23ede272-71d8-11e9-941d-97c0cfc7e867.html |archive-date=September 27, 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The control was enough that it operated within the United States as the legitimate state of Louisiana, electing members to the [[United States House of Representatives]]. With both governments being considered legitimate, both lines are included in all lists of governors. The schism ended when the Confederate governor fled and the whole state came under Union control.|name=schism}}

|rowspan="4" data-sort-value="1627"|June 27, 1868{{efn|Baker was removed, and Governor-elect Warmoth appointed as replacement, on June 27.<ref name="grant" /> Warmoth was formally inaugurated on July 13.<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 13, 1868 |title=Louisiana Legislature |page=1 |newspaper=[[The Times-Picayune/The New Orleans Advocate|The Daily Picayune]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-picayune-warmoth-inaugurated-j/130842935/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829041903/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-picayune-warmoth-inaugurated-j/130842935/ |archive-date=August 29, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>}}<br />–<br />December 9, 1872<br>{{small|(1627 days; removed)}}{{efn|During the [[1872 Louisiana gubernatorial election|1872 election]], Warmoth endorsed [[John McEnery (politician)|John McEnery]] for governor, and the State Returning Board, which he appointed, declared McEnery the winner. However, a rival board declared [[William Pitt Kellogg]] the winner, and the legislature impeached Warmoth on charges related to the election. Impeached officials are suspended from office, so at this time, P. B. S. Pinchback filled the office. The term expired only 35 days later, at which point impeachment charges were dropped, as Warmoth was no longer governor.{{sfn|Sobel|1978|p=572}}}}

|rowspan="2"|[[1872 Louisiana gubernatorial election|1872]]{{efn|The State Election Board certified McEnery as the winner of the 1872 election; however, a rival board declared Kellogg the winner, and the legislature went with that. Both McEnery and Kellogg declared victory and formed governments, and conflict culminated in the [[Battle of Liberty Place]] and the [[Colfax massacre]]. President [[Ulysses S. Grant]] issued a proclamation on May 22, 1873, declaring Kellogg the winner.<ref>{{Cite web |title=William Pitt Kellogg is officially named Governor of Louisiana by President Grant |url=https://historyengine.richmond.edu/episodes/view/49 |access-date=November 13, 2018 |website=[[University of Richmond]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240725124458/https://historyengine.richmond.edu/episodes/view/49 |archive-date=July 25, 2024 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |year=1874 |title=Statutes of the United States of America passed at the First Session of the Forty-Third Congress |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R08zAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PR3 |publisher=[[United States Government Publishing Office]] |at=Proclamation no. 1 |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref>|name=elect-1872}}

|rowspan="2" data-sort-value="1345"|May 21, 1928<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 21, 1928 |title=Huey P. Long Inaugurated |page=1 |newspaper=[[The Town Talk|Alexandria Daily Town Talk]] |agency=Associated Press |location=Baton Rouge, Louisiana |publication-place=Alexandria, Louisiana |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-town-talk-long-inaugurated-may-21/130919461/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230830162453/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-town-talk-long-inaugurated-may-21/130919461/ |archive-date=August 30, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><br>–<br>January 25, 1932<br>{{small|(1345 days; resigned)}}{{efn|Long was [[1930 United States Senate election in Louisiana|elected]] to the [[United States Senate]] for a term beginning March 4, 1931; however, he did not take the seat until January 25, 1932. This was in part to prevent Lieutenant Governor Cyr from replacing him as governor. When the senate term began, Cyr took the oath of office as governor and claimed the office; however, Long called this illegitimate, and said that by taking the oath of office of the governor, he had resigned from being lieutenant governor. This opened the way for the president pro tempore of the senate, Alvin Olin King, to become lieutenant governor, and ultimately succeed Long. Cyr continued to claim the office of governor on and off until 1932, but ultimately lacked recognition.<ref name="nga-king" />|name=king}}
